race.name: Imster Radmarathon
race.tagline: A timed 110 km Tyrolean road race with 2,300 m of climbing and a 1,000 m ascent packed into the Haimingerberg

vitals.start_format: Mass-participation road-race start at Agrarzentrum West; final 2027 start blocks are not yet published
vitals.registration: Open through the official organizer site, with online registration scheduled through May 21, 2027 at noon and race-office late entry subject to availability
vitals.entry_fee: Routes A and B: €56 through December 31, 2026; €66 through March 31, 2027; €76 through May 23; €80 on race day
vitals.feed_zones: Route A has aid at Haimingerberg/Sattele, Roppen, Jerzens/Gischlewies, and the finish
vitals.cutoff_time: Organizer control times: Telfs 09:20, Haimingerberg/Sattele 11:30, and Jerzens 14:30; final operational instructions govern
route_options: Route A: 110 km, 2,300 m climbing — Haimingerberg/Sattele, Oetz, and the Pitztal/Jerzens finish approach
Route B: 90 km, 1,300 m climbing — Mieminger Plateau, Inntal, and Pitztal/Jerzens
Panorama Route: 70 km, 700 m climbing — Mieminger Plateau, Telfs, Roppen, and the Imst Gorge return

climate.description: Late May in Tyrol can move quickly between cool valley starts, sun, rain, and colder exposed climbing or descending conditions. The 07:00 start and the route's movement between the Inn, Ötztal, and Pitztal corridors make adaptable layers and wet-road judgment part of the preparation.
challenges: Fast temperature changes between valleys and exposed climbs
Rain and reduced grip on long descents
Wind exposure across the Mieminger Plateau and Inntal

terrain.primary: Tyrolean valley roads with one severe sustained climb and repeated late rollers
terrain.surface: Paved public roads; the organizer states that the course remains open to normal traffic and Austrian road rules apply
features: Mieminger Plateau opening through Nassereith, Obsteig, and Mieming
Haimingerberg/Sattele: approximately 1,000 m of climbing in 10 km
Ochsengarten and Oetz transition after the main ascent
Pitztal return through Leins, Jerzens, Wenns, and Arzl
Timed control points at Telfs, Sattele, and Jerzens

fondo_rating.scoring_notes: Roadie Labs 14-dimension rubric. The confirmed 110 km distance scores as moderate, while 2,300 m of climbing and the concentrated Haimingerberg ascent create a genuine Alpine-Fondo demand. Transponder timing, age categories, four Route A aid points, useful inclusions, and strong Tyrolean scenery score well. Open public roads, regional rather than international prestige, an unannounced field size, and normal destination costs keep the race in Tier 3. Score verified from the dimension sum on 2026-08-15.

key_climbs: Holzleitensattel and Mieminger Plateau — the opening climbing sequence before Telfs
Haimingerberg/Sattele — approximately 1,000 m of climbing in 10 km
Pitztal to Jerzens — the late climbing sequence before Wenns, Arzl, and Imst
climb_profile.profile_type: Compact Alpine gran fondo with a severe central climb and late valley-wall fatigue
climb_profile.king_of_mountain: Haimingerberg/Sattele is the signature selection: the organizer describes roughly 1,000 vertical metres in 10 kilometres before the course turns through Ochsengarten and Oetz.

course_description.character: Route A starts at Agrarzentrum West and crosses the Mieminger Plateau through Nassereith, Obsteig, Mieming, and Telfs. After the Inntal section, the course commits to Haimingerberg/Sattele, where the organizer publishes approximately 1,000 vertical metres in only 10 kilometres. Riders then descend toward Oetz, cross the Ötztal corridor, and finish through the Pitztal towns of Leins, Jerzens, Wenns, and Arzl before returning to Imst.
course_description.signature_challenge: The race asks for Alpine climbing density rather than extreme distance. Riders must reach the Haimingerberg with enough threshold control to absorb a roughly 10-kilometre, 1,000-metre ascent, then descend safely, resume fueling, and still climb through the Pitztal late in a 110-kilometre day.
suffering_zones: Early positioning across the Mieminger Plateau
Cold or wet descent toward Oetz
Late Pitztal rise through Leins and Jerzens
Final return from Wenns and Arzl to Imst

logistics.airport: Innsbruck is the closest major airport; Imst is a regional Tyrolean town with rail and road access from the Inn Valley.
logistics.lodging_strategy: Book in Imst or nearby Brennbichl and confirm secure bicycle storage. Imst Tourism publishes certified bike accommodations with storage, washing, repair support, and local cycling information.
logistics.transport: Race packet pickup, start, finish, and post-race activity are based at Agrarzentrum West, Brennbichl 53. The organizer lists free participant and spectator parking nearby; the course itself remains open to traffic.
logistics.food: Route A publishes three on-course aid points plus finish support. The starter package includes a pasta voucher, and the pasta party begins at noon.

history.origin_story: The Imster Radmarathon grew into a recurring Tyrolean road-racing fixture organized by RC Radsportevents Tirol with Imst Tourism. The official site labels the May 23, 2027 edition as the 11th race and carries it within the Tiroler Rennradcup framework.
notable_moments: 2026: Route A results include a tightly contested men's podium and published women's classification despite isolated timing issues
2027: The 11th edition is scheduled for May 23 with three routes, open registration, and current course details
history.reputation: A demanding regional Alpine race with real timing, category classifications, and a hard course, but without the international field depth, closed roads, or global profile of Austria's Ötztaler Radmarathon.

biased_opinion.summary: Imst compresses an Alpine race into 110 kilometres. The main course is not long enough to hide behind steady endurance: the Haimingerberg demands sustained climbing power, the descent demands judgment, and the Pitztal return exposes every pacing and fueling mistake.
strengths: Exact 2027 date, registration window, Route A distance, climbing, start time, controls, and aid points are published
A genuine 2,300 m climbing load in only 110 km
Transponder timing, age classifications, and podium ceremonies
Three route lengths make the event accessible to mixed-ability groups
Entry includes a shirt, finisher medal, pasta voucher, and sponsor voucher
weaknesses: The course is open to traffic rather than fully closed
The organizer has not published a 2027 field-size target or final start blocks
The regional event lacks the deep international field and prestige of Austria's marquee fondos
Late-May mountain weather can complicate clothing and descending decisions
The hardest climbing arrives well before the finish, leaving a long sequence of smaller chances to unravel
biased_opinion.bottom_line: Choose Imst if you want a compact, hard Alpine race where climbing execution matters more than marquee status. Train the Haimingerberg as a sustained threshold problem and the Pitztal return as a fueling-and-durability problem.

final_verdict.one_liner: A timed 110 km Tyrolean race with 2,300 m of climbing, open roads, and one brutally concentrated Haimingerberg ascent.
final_verdict.should_you_race: Yes if you want serious Alpine climbing without a 200-kilometre day and are comfortable racing on roads that remain open to traffic. Skip if full closures, international prestige, or a large published field are essential to the experience.
final_verdict.alternatives: Ötztaler Radmarathon for Austria's iconic ultra-distance test, Engadin Radmarathon for a multi-day high-pass format, or Maratona dles Dolomites for deeper international prestige and fully developed event spectacle.
